questions.html: Which of the following is true about the relationship between $\text{LALR(1)}$ and $\text{SLR(1)}$ parsers?

options.html: There are grammars that can be parsed by $\text{SLR(1)}$ parsers that cannot be parsed by $\text{LALR(1)}$ parsers.

$\text{LALR(1)}$ parsers are as powerful as $\text{SLR(1)}$ parsers, so any grammar that can be parsed by an $\text{LALR(1)}$ parser can be parsed by a $\text{SLR(1)}$ parser.

For any grammar $\text{G}$ which can be parsed by a $\text{SLR(1)}$ parser, number of states in the $\text{SLR(1)}$ parser can be less than number of states in the $\text{LALR(1)}$ parser for $\text{G}$.

questions.html: Which of the following is true about grammar ambiguity?

options.html: A grammar is said to be ambiguous if it can produce more than one parse tree for some sentence/string.
A grammar is said to be ambiguous when, for some sentence, two different sequences of leftmost derivations can produce the same sentence from the same start symbol.
A grammar is ambiguous if there is some string $w$ such that $w\text{’s}$ right-most derivation differs from its left-most derivation.
A grammar is said to be ambiguous if and only if, for some sentence, two different sequences of rightmost derivations can produce the same sentence from the same start symbol.

questions.solution:

questions.html:

$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { State 0: } & \text { State 2: } \\

{[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{c}]} & {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{b}]} \\

\end{array}
$$
$$\begin{array}{ll}\text { State 1: } & \text { State } 3: \\ {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{a}]} & {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} \\ {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} & {[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} \\ {[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{b}]} & \end{array}$$

questions.html:
Consider the following sets of $\text{LR(1)}$ items in the states of a $\text{LR(1)}$ parser for some grammar $\text{G}.$
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { State 0: } & \text { State 2: } \\
{[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} & {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{c}]} \\
{[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{c}]} & {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{b}]} \\
{[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{b}]} & {[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{a}]}
\end{array}
$$
$$
\begin{array}{ll}
\text { State 1: } & \text { State } 3: \\
{[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{a}]} & {[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} \\
{[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} & {[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]} \\
{[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{b}]} &
\end{array}
$$
Which of the following is true for the given set of $\text{LR1}$ items and the given $\text{LR1}$ parser (Assume the parser has only the given set of $\text{LR1}$ items for $\text{G)}?$

options.html: $\text{G}$ is not $\text{LR1}$ because reduce/reduce conflict is caused by $\left[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{a}{\bullet}, \mathrm{c}\right]$ and $[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{b}]$ in state $1.$

$\text{G}$ is not $\text{LR1}$ because Shift/reduce conflict is caused by $[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{c}]$ and $[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \mathrm{a} \bullet, \mathrm{a}]$ on lookahead $\mathrm{a}$ in state $2.$

$\text{G}$ is not $\text{LR1}$ because Shift/shift conflict is caused by $[\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]$ and $[\mathrm{B} \rightarrow \bullet \mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}]$ on lookahead $\mathrm{a}$ in state $3.$

We have a scanner (lexical analyzer) "flex". Consider the following tokens and their associated regular expressions, given as a flex scanner specification :
$$\begin{array}{|l|l|}
\hline \text { Regular expression } & \text { Token }\\
\hline(01 \mid 10) & \text{printf(“ }\mathrm{X} \text { ") }\\
\hline 0(01)^{\ast} 1 & \text{printf(“ Y ")}\\
\hline\left(1010^{\ast} 1 \mid 0101^{\ast} 0\right) & \text{printf(“ Z ") }\\
\hline
\end{array}$$
When using regular expressions to scan an input, we resolve conflicts by taking the largest possible match at any point. If two longest matches are of same length then we give preference in the below order $: \mathrm{X}>\mathrm{Y}>\mathrm{Z}$

For Which of the following inputs to this scanner, we will get a Lexical error?
questions.solution:
Answer: B, C

Official discussion page

questions.html:
In lexical analysis, when using regular expressions to scan an input, for resolving conflicts that occur, our approach is usually to use "maximal­-munch" (i.e. to always choose the longest possible match at any point), and if, even with maximal-munch we have multiple matching regular expressions, then we break ties based on the priorities of the regular expressions.


Consider the following scanner (lexical analyzer) “flex”.
Consider the following tokens and their associated regular expressions, given as a flex scanner specification :
$$
\begin{array}{|c|l|}
\hline \text{Regular expression} & \text{Token}\\
\hline aa & \text{print(“1")}\\
\hline a &\text{print( “2")}\\
\hline ab & \text{print(“3")}\\
\hline
\end{array}$$
If two longest matches are of same length then we give preference in the below order : $1>2>3$
 

For which of the following input strings: The string can be broken apart into substrings, where each substring matches one of the regular expressions, but $\bullet$ The maximal-munch algorithm will fail to break the string apart in a way where each piece matches one of the regular expressions.
questions.solution:
Answer: B
